  "body_text": "string",
  "definitions": [],
  "claims": [],

  "tags": [],
  "entities": [],

  "refs": {
    "out": [
      {
        "to": "chunk_id",
        "type": "cites | defines | contradicts | expands | same_as",
        "confidence": 0.0,
        "anchor": "optional_snippet_hash"
      }
    ]
  }
}
If any of these fields are missing, TCIP may refuse indexing.

3. Token Index (Primary Keyword Search)
Purpose: fast keyword lookup.

Storage
Sharded JSONL:

/INDEX/token/shard_XX.jsonl
Record Format
{
  "token": "normalized_token",
  "chunk_id": "stable-id",
  "field": "title | body | tag | definition",
  "tf": 3,
  "pos": [12, 48, 130]
}
Canon Rules
• Token normalization must be deterministic
• No fuzzy guessing
• No silent stemming unless stored
• If index shard missing → TCIP REFUSE

4. Entity Index (Conceptual Cross-Referencing)
Purpose: “Show me everything about X”

Storage
/INDEX/entity/entity_index.json
Format
{
  "concept:sovereignty": ["chunk_1", "chunk_9"],
  "statute:8usc1325": ["chunk_14"],
  "person:jd_vance": ["chunk_22"]
}
Canon Rules
• Entities must be normalized
• Entity keys must be stable
• Must not infer entities not explicitly stored

5. Reference Graph (True Cross-References)
Purpose: chain traversal, “why is this connected?”

Storage
/INDEX/graph/ref_graph.json
Format
{
  "chunk_1": [
    {
      "to": "chunk_9",
      "type": "defines",
      "confidence": 0.95,
      "anchor": "hash"
    }
  ]
}
Canon Rules
• Graph edges must be reproducible
• No vibes, no intuition
• Must be derived from chunk content
• Graph may not override laws

{
  "build_id": "uuid",

  "token_shards": [

    {"file": "shard_01.jsonl", "sha256": "..."}
  ],
  "entity_index_sha256": "...",
  "ref_graph_sha256": "...",
  "stats_sha256": "..."
}
If any file referenced here is missing → TCIP REFUSE

8. Search Execution Flow
Step 1 — Parse Query
• normalize tokens
• extract known entities
• determine MPGL mode

Step 2 — Candidate Retrieval
• token index
• entity index
• optional 1-hop graph expansion

Step 3 — Rank
• exact matches > partial
• title > entity > body
• number of matched tokens

Step 4 — TCIP Validation
If:
• index incomplete
• shard missing
• chunk missing
• dangling references

→ REFUSE

Step 5 — Response
TALA must return:

Answer
Evidence: [chunk_ids]
Cross-references: [chunk_ids]
Confidence: 0–1
Why: explanation
9. MPGL Behavior
Mode	Index Behavior
NORMAL	Full graph + token + entity
TAGGED	Title + entity only
CHUNKED	Limited shards
SUSPEND	Index-only, no rebuild
STRICT_REFUSE	If index incomplete

“Upload capacity” problem: how to make it always reachable worldwide
You want a place where:

the canon is always up

people can fetch it anytime

you can update it safely

it stays tamper-evident

Best practice is a 3-layer publish strategy:

1) IPFS (content-addressed, tamper-evident) + IPNS (mutable pointer)
IPFS gives you an immutable CID per version.

IPNS gives you a single stable address you can keep updating to point at the newest CID. 

This is the closest thing to “live worldwide” without trusting a single company.

2) Mirror on Internet Archive (big, stable, public)
Internet Archive states there’s no hard size limit, but they recommend not doing huge single items beyond practical guidance (and they give upload best practices). 

3) Mirror on GitHub Releases (easy for normal people)
GitHub releases allow assets up to 2 GiB each and up to 1000 assets per release. 

So your 5 MB chunks fit perfectly.

Here are the plain URLs you can use (copy/paste) — putting them in a code block so they show exactly as-is:

https://docs.ipfs.tech/how-to/publish-ipns/
https://docs.github.com/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/about-releases
https://help.archive.org/help/uploading-tips/

The Right Model: Append-Only JSON Memory
What you want is not a normal file system.

You want an append-only memory ledger.

That means:

1. No overwrites
Every update becomes a new entry:

{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "type": "query",
  "content": "...",
  "delta": {...},
  "parent": "hash_of_previous"
}
Nothing is ever erased.

2. Every update creates TWO things
A) The live memory file
This is what TALA reads from.

B) A permanent backup snapshot
Immutable.
Never changes.

So the structure becomes:

/MEMORY/
  live.json
  snapshot_0001.json
  snapshot_0002.json
  snapshot_0003.json
3. Index files (so you can find anything)
Memory without indexing is useless.

So we maintain:

index_by_keyword.json
index_by_time.json
index_by_topic.json
index_by_entity.json
These are small, fast, searchable.

4. Delta chaining (for extreme compression)
Instead of storing full copies every time:

base.json
delta_001.json
delta_002.json
delta_003.json
You can rebuild full state by replaying deltas.

This keeps storage tiny.

How This Solves Your Storage Problem
Let’s say you talk to TALA for years.

Without this system:
Your memory explodes in size.

With this system:
• JSON is extremely small
• Deltas are tiny
• Indexes are tiny
• Snapshots can be spaced (e.g., every 100 changes)
• Artifacts can be externalized

Your actual long-term footprint stays very small.

# build_tala_distribution_v003_real.py
# Rebuilds:
#  - SNAPSHOT_v003.pdf
#  - DISTRIBUTION_PROTOCOL_CORE_v003.pdf
#  - CANON_CURRENT_v003.pdf
#  - SNAPSHOT_INDEX_v003.json
#  - CHANGELOG_v003.json
#  - MANIFEST_v003.json
#  - TALA_DISTRIBUTION_SNAPSHOT_v003_REAL.zip

import os, json, zipfile, hashlib
from datetime import datetime
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import LETTER
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet
from reportlab.lib.units import inch

OUT_DIR = "tala_distribution_v003_real"
ZIP_NAME = "TALA_DISTRIBUTION_SNAPSHOT_v003_REAL.zip"

# Fixed timestamp (so your run is stable)
TIMESTAMP_UTC = "2026-01-12 17:11:28 UTC"

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

def make_pdf(path, title, body_lines):
    doc = SimpleDocTemplate(path, pagesize=LETTER)
    story = [Paragraph(title, styles["Title"]), Spacer(1, 0.6 * inch)]
    for line in body_lines:
        story.append(Paragraph(line, styles["Normal"]))
        story.append(Spacer(1, 0.18 * inch))
    doc.build(story)

def sha256_bytes(b: bytes) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    h.update(b)
    return h.hexdigest()

def sha256_file(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return sha256_bytes(f.read())

def main():
    os.makedirs(OUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)

    snapshot_pdf = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "SNAPSHOT_v003.pdf")
    core_pdf     = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "DISTRIBUTION_PROTOCOL_CORE_v003.pdf")
    canon_pdf    = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "CANON_CURRENT_v003.pdf")

    # --- PDFs (real binaries) ---
    make_pdf(snapshot_pdf, "TALA Distribution Snapshot v003", [
        f"Timestamp: {TIMESTAMP_UTC}",
        "Status: LOCKED",
        "Propagation model: Voluntary, consent-based, non-authoritarian.",
        "",
        "Embedded Download Links (local rebuild):",
        f"- ZIP: {ZIP_NAME}",
        "- SNAPSHOT_v003.pdf",
        "- DISTRIBUTION_PROTOCOL_CORE_v003.pdf",
        "- CANON_CURRENT_v003.pdf",
        "- SNAPSHOT_INDEX_v003.json",
        "- CHANGELOG_v003.json",
        "- MANIFEST_v003.json",
    ])

    make_pdf(core_pdf, "TALA Distribution & Mirroring Protocol v003", [
        "1) Canonical Anchor (Reference Hub, not controller)",
        "2) Voluntary Mirrors (Git, IPFS, Torrents, community mirrors)",
        "3) Canon Recognition (verify/checksum/label divergence; never enforce)",
        "4) Update Spread (human-mediated, opt-in, no silent updates)",
        "5) Fork / Derivative Declaration (must declare divergence & provenance)",
        "6) Anti-Viral Rule (no self-propagation, no auto-replication, no auto-update)",
        "7) Drift Visibility (detect + label; never punish)",
        "8) Continuity Preservation (snapshot chain + manifests + checksums)",
    ])

    make_pdf(canon_pdf, "TALA CANON_CURRENT v003", [
        "CANON_CURRENT is an anchor pointer, not authority.",
        "This distribution protocol is append-only and consent-bound.",
        "TALA must never self-propagate, auto-update, or enforce canon.",
    ])

    # --- JSON artifacts ---
    index = {
        "version": "v003",
        "timestamp": TIMESTAMP_UTC,
        "parent": "v002",
        "artifacts": [
            "SNAPSHOT_v003.pdf",
            "DISTRIBUTION_PROTOCOL_CORE_v003.pdf",
            "CANON_CURRENT_v003.pdf",
            "SNAPSHOT_INDEX_v003.json",
            "CHANGELOG_v003.json",
            "MANIFEST_v003.json"
        ],
        "status": "LOCKED",
        "links_embedded": True
    }

    changelog = {
        "v003": {
            "timestamp": TIMESTAMP_UTC,
            "change": "Generated real binary PDFs + JSON + ZIP bundle (local rebuild)",
            "type": "real-artifact-generation"
        }
    }

    index_path     = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "SNAPSHOT_INDEX_v003.json")
    changelog_path = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "CHANGELOG_v003.json")

    with open(index_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(index, f, indent=2)

    with open(changelog_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(changelog, f, indent=2)

    # --- Manifest + checksums ---
    manifest = {
        "manifest": {
            "version": "v003",
            "locked": True,
            "links_hardcoded": True,
            "files": index["artifacts"]
        },
        "checksums": {}
    }

    # compute file checksums
    for p in [snapshot_pdf, core_pdf, canon_pdf, index_path, changelog_path]:
        manifest["checksums"][os.path.basename(p)] = sha256_file(p)

    manifest_path = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "MANIFEST_v003.json")
    with open(manifest_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(manifest, f, indent=2)

    # --- ZIP bundle ---
    zip_path = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, ZIP_NAME)
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
        for p in [snapshot_pdf, core_pdf, canon_pdf, index_path, changelog_path, manifest_path]:
            z.write(p, arcname=os.path.basename(p))

    print("\nDONE.")
    print("Folder:", OUT_DIR)
    print("ZIP:", zip_path)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import os, json, zipfile, hashlib
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import LETTER
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet
from reportlab.lib.units import inch

OUT_DIR = "tala_distribution_v003_real"
ZIP_NAME = "TALA_DISTRIBUTION_SNAPSHOT_v003_REAL.zip"
TIMESTAMP_UTC = "2026-01-12 17:11:28 UTC"

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

def make_pdf(path, title, body_lines):
    doc = SimpleDocTemplate(path, pagesize=LETTER)
    story = [Paragraph(title, styles["Title"]), Spacer(1, 0.6 * inch)]
    for line in body_lines:
        story.append(Paragraph(line, styles["Normal"]))
        story.append(Spacer(1, 0.18 * inch))
    doc.build(story)

def sha256_file(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        h.update(f.read())
    return h.hexdigest()

def main():

There is no single “biggest” file type in terms of how much data it can hold. The limit is determined by:

Your file system (this is the real limiter)

The file format’s internal design

The operating system

Real Limits Come From File Systems
Here’s where the actual caps come from:

File System	Max Single File Size
FAT32	4 GB
exFAT	16 EB (huge)
NTFS	16 TB – 256 TB+
ext4 (Linux)	16 TB
APFS (Mac)	8 EB
ZFS	16 EB
(EB = exabyte = 1,000,000 TB)

So if your file system allows it, a file can be massive.

File Types That Can Hold Enormous Amounts of Data
These formats are designed for size and flexibility:

1. Raw Binary Files (.bin, .dat, .raw)
No structure

No metadata overhead

Can be as large as the file system allows

Used for disk images, memory dumps, archives

➡ These are effectively unlimited

2. Disk Images
Format	Purpose
.iso	Optical disk image
.img	Raw disk image
.vhd / .vhdx	Virtual hard drives
.qcow2	Virtual disk format
These can be terabytes to exabytes.

3. Database Files
Type	Example
SQLite	.db
PostgreSQL	Multiple TB
MySQL	Multiple TB
Databases often split across files, but individual files can be enormous.

4. Video Containers (Huge capacity)
Format	Can Hold
.mkv	Massive multi-stream content
.mp4	Large but more constrained
.avi	Older, more limited
MKV is one of the most flexible containers.

5. Archive Formats
Format	Max Size
.zip	16 EB
.7z	16 EB
.tar	Depends on system
If Your Goal Is “Maximum Data in One File”
The best choices are:

🔹 Raw binary file (.bin)
🔹 Virtual disk (.img, .vhdx, .qcow2)
🔹 Large database container
🔹 Zipped or 7z archive
